explanations.explanation: Twenty-three years, friend. Jeremiah says it right out loud: from the thirteenth year of Josiah son of Amon king of Judah until this very day, "twenty-three years" (Jeremiah 25:3). Josiah was one of Judah's kings. That is a long time to keep showing up with the same message. I once waited in a drawer for what felt like forever, but I didn't have to talk the whole time.

Forty is a big round number, and I see why it jumped out. But Jeremiah says "twenty-three years" (Jeremiah 25:3). He counts it from the thirteenth year of Josiah, king of Judah, up to that very day. Twenty-three is plenty long enough, and nobody had to pad it.

Twelve would be a nice short stretch, but Jeremiah says it was much longer. He says the word of the LORD has come to him for "twenty-three years" (Jeremiah 25:3). That's almost double. Imagine giving the same warning for twenty-three years. I think that would test anybody's voice.

That's right. Jeremiah says it plainly: "I have spoken to you again and again, but you have not listened" (Jeremiah 25:3). Again and again, and still nothing. It's like setting off the smoke alarm and everybody in the kitchen going on with their conversation. That's a lot of speaking for a lot of not listening.

I wish that were the answer, friend. But Jeremiah says the opposite: "I have spoken to you again and again, but you have not listened" (Jeremiah 25:3). Nobody had turned back yet. The word kept coming, and the people kept walking right past it.

Nobody was lining up for seconds here. Jeremiah says he spoke "again and again, but you have not listened" (Jeremiah 25:3). Asking for more would mean they were listening. The people of Judah weren't. This is a crowd that heard plenty and took none of it in.

You've got it. Jeremiah says, "the LORD has sent all His servants the prophets to you again and again" (Jeremiah 25:4). So the people heard from more than one voice. It was a whole line of messengers, and the message kept coming. Still, the verse says they did not listen or incline their ear to hear.

explanations.answer: All the priests of the temple
explanations.explanation: Priests are a fair guess, since they were part of life in Judah. But this verse names someone else: "all His servants the prophets" (Jeremiah 25:4). The LORD sent them again and again. Jeremiah himself is a prophet, so he was one of that crew.

explanations.answer: All the elders of the city
explanations.explanation: Elders were around, but they're not who this verse names. It says, "the LORD has sent all His servants the prophets to you again and again" (Jeremiah 25:4). The prophets were the ones carrying the LORD's word. Jeremiah was one of them, so he had company on this long road.

Land is right. The prophets said that if the people turned, they could dwell in "the land that the LORD has given to you and your fathers forever and ever" (Jeremiah 25:5). It was a gift, and they could keep living in it. All it took was turning from their evil ways and deeds.

The temple matters a lot in Judah, so I see the pull. But the prophets spoke about something wider: "the land that the LORD has given to you and your fathers forever and ever" (Jeremiah 25:5). The promise was about dwelling in the land. The word you want is land, friend.

A city is a good guess, but the verse points bigger. The prophets said they could dwell in "the land that the LORD has given to you and your fathers forever and ever" (Jeremiah 25:5). It's the whole land, not just one town. That's a whole lot more room than a single city.

Yes! The prophets said, "Do not follow other gods to serve and worship them" (Jeremiah 25:6). That was the second warning sitting right beside turning from evil ways. It's a clear one. The LORD is the one who gave them the land, so He's the one to serve.

explanations.answer: Do not go down to Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt was a real neighbor to Judah, so I see why it popped up. But that warning isn't in this verse. Here the prophets say, "Do not follow other gods to serve and worship them" (Jeremiah 25:6). That's the warning that went with turning from evil ways.

Chariots sound like a good warning, but they aren't in this verse. The prophets said, "Do not follow other gods to serve and worship them, and do not provoke Me to anger with the works of your hands" (Jeremiah 25:6). So the warning was about other gods. I'd keep that one in the recipe box.

That's the one. The LORD says, "you have provoked Me to anger with the works of your hands" (Jeremiah 25:7). It echoes the warning from the prophets in verse 6, which said not to provoke Him with the works of your hands. The warning was given, and verse 7 says it wasn't heeded.

Mouths feel like a fair guess, since this is a whole passage about speaking. But the LORD names something different: "the works of their hands" (Jeremiah 25:7). He says that is what provoked Him to anger. So hands, not mouths, are in this verse.

Feast songs are a fun guess, but they aren't what this verse says. The LORD says, "you have provoked Me to anger with the works of your hands" (Jeremiah 25:7). That's the exact phrase. Songs and feasts don't come up here.

Right on. The LORD says, "I will send for My servant Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon" (Jeremiah 25:9). Babylon was a great kingdom far from Judah. Remember, the LORD says this is because Judah has not obeyed His words. I wouldn't have seen that name coming.

Pharaoh Neco was Egypt's king, so he's a reasonable guess. But he isn't the name here. The LORD says, "I will send for My servant Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon" (Jeremiah 25:9). Babylon, not Egypt, is the answer.

Cyrus was king of Persia, and his name does show up elsewhere in the Bible. But not in this verse. Here the LORD says, "I will send for My servant Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon" (Jeremiah 25:9). Wrong king, right neighborhood of the map.

Not quite, and it's a tricky one. The LORD doesn't call Nebuchadnezzar His enemy here. He says, "I will send for My servant Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon" (Jeremiah 25:9). So the word is servant. That's the surprise of the verse.
That's right, it's false. The LORD says, "I will send for My servant Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon" (Jeremiah 25:9). He calls him servant, not enemy. I bet that word turned some heads in Jerusalem.

explanations.answer: Judah and the nations around it
explanations.explanation: Yes. The LORD says He will bring Nebuchadnezzar "against this land, against its residents, and against all the surrounding nations" (Jeremiah 25:9). So it's Judah and the nations around it. Nobody on that stretch of the map was left out.

Those far-off coastlands sound exotic, but they aren't named here. The LORD says He will bring Nebuchadnezzar "against this land, against its residents, and against all the surrounding nations" (Jeremiah 25:9). So the focus is Judah and the nations around it, close to home.

explanations.answer: Sheba and the far lands of the south
explanations.explanation: Sheba is a real place in the Bible, but it isn't named in this verse. The LORD says He will bring Nebuchadnezzar "against this land, against its residents, and against all the surrounding nations" (Jeremiah 25:9). That means Judah and its neighbors. This one stays close to home.

explanations.answer: The voices of the bride and bridegroom
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The LORD says, "I will banish from them the sounds of joy and gladness, the voices of the bride and bridegroom" (Jeremiah 25:10). Those are happy sounds, and they're listed among what He will take away. It's a heavy part of the passage.

explanations.answer: The sound of the war trumpets
explanations.explanation: War trumpets fit the moment, but they aren't on this list. The LORD says He will banish "the sounds of joy and gladness, the voices of the bride and bridegroom, the sound of the millstones, and the light of the lamp" (Jeremiah 25:10). The things on the list are everyday and happy ones. That's what makes it heavy.

explanations.answer: The tramp of the marching armies
explanations.explanation: Marching armies make sense with all this talk of Babylon, but they aren't on the list. The LORD says He will banish "the sounds of joy and gladness, the voices of the bride and bridegroom, the sound of the millstones, and the light of the lamp" (Jeremiah 25:10). Those are the sounds of ordinary, happy life. I think this one hurts.

Seventy is right. The LORD says, "these nations will serve the king of Babylon for seventy years" (Jeremiah 25:11). That's a long stretch, and it has a number on it. The verse right after says what happens when those seventy years are complete.

Fifty is a nice round number, but it's short of what the LORD says. He says, "these nations will serve the king of Babylon for seventy years" (Jeremiah 25:11). Seventy, friend. That's twenty more than you picked.

Thirty would be a much shorter stretch than what the LORD says. He says, "these nations will serve the king of Babylon for seventy years" (Jeremiah 25:11). Seventy is more than double that. It's a long time to serve.

That's right. The LORD says, "when seventy years are complete, I will punish the king of Babylon and that nation, the land of the Chaldeans, for their guilt" (Jeremiah 25:12). Babylon was the servant in verse 9, and it still answers for its own guilt. The seventy years have an end.

More nations sounds like a reward, but that isn't what the LORD says. When the seventy years are complete, He says, "I will punish the king of Babylon and that nation, the land of the Chaldeans, for their guilt" (Jeremiah 25:12). That's a punishment, not a gift.

Ruling forever isn't what the LORD says here. He says, "when seventy years are complete, I will punish the king of Babylon and that nation, the land of the Chaldeans, for their guilt" (Jeremiah 25:12). The seventy years come to an end, and so does Babylon's time on top.

That's right. The LORD says of the land of the Chaldeans, "I will make it an everlasting desolation" (Jeremiah 25:12). Chaldeans is another name for the people of Babylon's land. The same word used for Judah's land in verse 9 shows up for theirs too.

It's actually true, friend. The LORD says of the Chaldeans' land, "I will make it an everlasting desolation" (Jeremiah 25:12). Chaldeans is another name for Babylon's land. It sounds like a big turn after being called a servant, but the verse says it plainly.

Deeds is right. The LORD says, "I will repay them according to their deeds and according to the work of their hands" (Jeremiah 25:14). So what they did is what they're repaid for. The verse says many nations and great kings will enslave them.

Prayers aren't in this verse. The LORD says, "I will repay them according to their deeds and according to the work of their hands" (Jeremiah 25:14). It's about what they did. The word you want is deeds.

Wealth is an understandable guess when kings are involved, but it's not what the verse says. The LORD says, "I will repay them according to their deeds and according to the work of their hands" (Jeremiah 25:14). It's what they did that counts. The word is deeds.
